teaser: An angel lands in a tidy Flemish living room, and next door a carpenter is building mousetraps.
review_notes:
Date given in metadata as 1428; the Met dates it ca. 1427-32 and attributes it to the workshop of Robert Campin.
Overall size open: 64.5 x 117.8 cm (Met).
Donor identified as Peter Engelbrecht (Ingelbrechts/Inghelbrechts) of Mechelen from the coat of arms in the window; the pun on 'Engel' (angel) in his name is a common suggestion, not a proven motive.
Wife and the messenger at the gate added later; central window originally gold, later painted with sky and coats of arms: per Met technical study.
Mousetrap interpretation: Meyer Schapiro, 1945, citing Saint Augustine.
The object on the outside window ledge is usually also called a mousetrap; the board Joseph drills has been read as a foot-warmer lid, a strainer for a winepress or a spike block: unresolved.
Table described as sixteen-sided (Met).
Rogier van der Weyden and Jacques Daret documented as Campin's apprentices in Tournai.
Met purchase for The Cloisters in 1956; previously with the Arenberg and Merode families.
The image includes the gilded frame; all coordinates are relative to the full image with frame.

lesson.text: An angel with gold and green wings has just come into the room. The air he pushed ahead of him has blown out the candle on the table. And the young woman he came to see has not looked up from her book. In this picture the biggest news in Christian history arrives, and for one more second nobody has noticed.

There is a second thing that does not add up. The Annunciation, the moment the angel Gabriel tells Mary she will bear the son of God, took place in Nazareth some fourteen centuries before this was painted. Yet the bench, the shutters, the brass and the tiled floor are those of a comfortable townhouse in Flanders around 1430.

The object itself is modest. It is a triptych, a painting in three hinged panels, and the whole thing open is about 65 centimeters high and 118 wide (26 by 46 inches). The wings fold shut like a cupboard. It was never meant for a church. Someone bought it to pray in front of at home.
Back to that room. Gabriel is not the only one arriving. A third traveler is on the way in, much smaller, and easy to take for a fleck of paint.
Someone tiny is flying into the central room. Where?

spots.title: A child with a cross
spots.text: A naked infant slides down golden rays from the round window, heading for Mary. He already carries a cross on his shoulder. He has come through the glass without breaking it.

lesson.text: That last detail was a sermon in itself. Preachers compared Mary's virginity to a window: light passes through and the glass stays whole. And the little cross tells you the end of the story on its very first day. Once you know that objects here can speak, the whole room starts talking.

spots.title: Lilies in a jug
spots.text: White lilies stand for Mary's purity. They sit in an ordinary blue and white pottery jug, the kind a Flemish household really owned.

spots.title: The snuffed candle
spots.text: The wick has just gone out and a thread of smoke still rises. One reading: ordinary light gives way when divine light enters the room.

spots.title: Kettle and towel
spots.text: A brass water vessel hangs in a niche with a clean towel beside it: a washing corner. It doubles as an image of purity, and a chance to paint light on polished metal.

spots.title: A book left open
spots.text: Its pages lift as if caught by the same gust that put out the candle. A green cloth pouch lies under it, the travel cover of a prayer book.

spots.title: Sitting low
spots.text: Mary does not sit on the bench. She sits on the floor in front of it, leaning back against the seat. In the language of the time, that low position means humility.

spots.title: Gabriel
spots.text: He kneels in white with a blue sash, one hand raised to speak. His wings are squeezed between the table and the wall, as if the room were a size too small for him.

lesson.text: Did the table look odd to you? Its top tips toward us so steeply that the jug and book ought to slide off. The rules of perspective, the geometry that makes a flat surface look deep, were being worked out in Italy in these same years. This painter went by eye, and preferred showing you every object to getting the angles right.

The patch of sky in the back window is a later idea. Technical study at the Metropolitan Museum showed the window was first covered in gold leaf, the old way of painting heaven. It was then painted over with clouds, and two coats of arms were added to the glass.

Now the right wing, which may be the most original of the three. Joseph, Mary's husband, usually stands at the edge of holy pictures, an old man with nothing to do. Here he gets a workshop of his own, a bench full of tools, and a view over the town.

lesson.title: Joseph's workshop
lesson.text: He is a carpenter, hard at work, and looking at nothing but his hands.

spots.title: On the bench
spots.text: Among the chisels and pliers sits a small wooden contraption with a wire spring. It is a mousetrap, finished and ready.

spots.title: Shop display
spots.text: A second device sits out on the ledge of the open shop window, facing the street, the way a craftsman showed his goods to passers-by.

spots.title: The drill
spots.text: With a hand drill called an auger, he bores rows of holes into a board held on his knee. What the board is for remains an open puzzle.

spots.title: The square
spots.text: Stepped gables, church spires, people crossing a market square. No such place existed in Nazareth. It is a Netherlandish town, painted smaller than a postage stamp.

lesson.text: Why mousetraps? For centuries nobody could say. In 1945 the American historian Meyer Schapiro found the key in a sermon by Saint Augustine, written a thousand years before the painting: the cross was a mousetrap set for the devil, and Christ's death was the bait. Joseph is quietly building the trap.

The board with the holes has never been settled. Scholars have proposed the lid of a foot warmer, a strainer for pressing grapes, and a block of spikes that appears in scenes of Christ carrying the cross. Three theories, one plank.

The left wing belongs to the people who paid. They kneel in a walled garden, at a door left ajar, and look in on the miracle. Painting yourself at the edge of a holy scene was a way of praying permanently. These buyers are known as donors.

lesson.title: At the door
lesson.text: Three people, and only one of them was there from the start.

spots.title: The husband
spots.text: Hat in hand, eyes wide, he stares through the open door. He is thought to be Peter Engelbrecht, a merchant from the town of Mechelen.

spots.title: The wife
spots.text: She was added afterward, squeezed in behind him, probably when he married. Her eyes are lowered and she holds a string of red prayer beads.

spots.title: The man at the gate
spots.text: Far back by the street door stands a bearded man with a badge on his chest, most likely a town messenger. He too is an addition, and no one is sure why he is there.

lesson.text: So the picture grew with the family that owned it. As for its maker, the name on the label is a careful one: workshop of Robert Campin. Campin ran a busy studio in Tournai, in today's Belgium, and signed nothing. Several hands may have shared this work. One of his apprentices, Rogier van der Weyden, became the most admired painter of the next generation.
The new idea here is that the sacred can happen in a room like yours. Every household object is real enough to touch, and at the same time means something more.

The triptych is named after the Mérode family, Belgian aristocrats who owned it in the nineteenth century. It stayed in private hands, rarely seen, until the Metropolitan Museum bought it in 1956 for The Cloisters, its branch for medieval art in New York.

quiz.question: What is a triptych?
options: A painting made on three hinged panels
A painting made by three artists
quiz.explanation: A triptych has three panels; here the wings can fold shut over the center.

quiz.question: What does the tiny child flying toward Mary carry?
quiz.explanation: The infant slides down the rays with a small cross on his shoulder.

quiz.question: According to Meyer Schapiro, why is Joseph making mousetraps?
options: Flemish houses were full of mice
A sermon by Saint Augustine called the cross a mousetrap for the devil
It was the painter's own trade
quiz.explanation: Schapiro linked the traps to Augustine's image of the cross as the devil's mousetrap.

quiz.question: Why does Mary sit on the floor instead of the bench?
options: She is hiding from the angel
Sitting low is a sign of humility

quiz.question: What was the triptych made for?
options: The main altar of a cathedral
quiz.explanation: It is small, folds shut, and was bought for prayer at home.

facts.text: The donor's wife was part of the left wing from the very beginning.
facts.explanation: She was added later, probably when the donor married.

facts.text: The sky in the central room's window was originally gold.
facts.explanation: Technical study showed gold leaf under the painted clouds.

facts.text: Robert Campin signed the central panel in the lower corner.
facts.explanation: Campin signed nothing, which is why the work is given to his workshop.
